## The idea

Three notes can organise a much longer melody if their relationships survive
change. Repeat the cell higher and the connection remains exposed. Double its
durations and recognition becomes slower, though the shape is still present.
Keep only its first two notes and even the fragment can point back to the source.

A *motive* is a short musical idea that remains recognisable under some
transformation. A *sequence* restates it at another pitch level. *Development*
uses operations such as transposition, inversion, augmentation, and fragmentation
to make repeated material acquire new consequences. A literal statement tells
the listener what the object is; later changes reveal how far its identity can
bend without breaking.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 108
use_synth :pluck

cell = [60, 63, 62]
rhythm = [0.5, 0.5, 1]

define :play_phrase do |notes, durations|
  notes.zip(durations).each do |pitch, duration|
    play pitch, release: duration * 0.8
    sleep duration
  end
end

define :transpose_notes do |notes, amount|
  notes.map { |pitch| pitch + amount }
end

define :invert_notes do |notes, axis|
  notes.map { |pitch| axis - (pitch - axis) }
end

bars = [
  [cell, rhythm],
  [transpose_notes(cell, 2), rhythm],
  [transpose_notes(cell, 5), rhythm],
  [invert_notes(cell, cell[0]), rhythm],
  [cell, rhythm.map { |duration| duration * 2 }],
  [cell.first(2) * 2, [0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5]],
  [transpose_notes(invert_notes(cell, cell[0]), 7), rhythm],
  [[60, 63, 62, 60], [0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5]]
]

2.times do
  bars.each { |notes, durations| play_phrase notes, durations }
end
```

The opening cell returns at new pitch levels, reflected around an axis, stretched
to twice its duration, and reduced to a fragment. Repeat the eight-bar plan and
one source object supplies a sixteen-bar melody. Listen for recognition arriving
at different speeds: transposition announces itself quickly, while inversion or
fragmentation may become clear only after the cell has finished.

## Change one thing

1. Replace sequence offsets `2` and `5` with `1` and `2`. The successive entries
   now crowd together. Notice whether they merge into one rising thought instead
   of sounding like statements made at distinct levels.
2. Move the inversion axis from the first note to 63. Reflection preserves the
   signed-distance rule but places the result in another register, showing that
   an operation and its chosen reference are separate decisions.
3. Repeat the unaltered cell four times. Mark the point, if there is one, when
   repetition stops confirming the idea and begins to hold the music still.
   Then compare that span with the developed version.

## Why it works

Transposition adds one constant to all pitches and preserves every interval.
Inversion reflects signed distances around an axis, turning an upward minor
third into a downward one. Augmentation scales duration; fragmentation selects
a subsequence. Each transformation keeps certain invariants and releases others,
which is why the motive can remain present without returning unchanged.

The `bars` array holds compositional decisions while `play_phrase` handles their
realisation. Transformed passages derive from `cell` rather than copied literals,
so changing the source also changes its descendants. That is musically useful:
you can revise the identity of the motive and hear the whole piece respond,
instead of repairing scattered imitations by hand.

A sequence becomes legible through recurrence at successive pitch levels. Two
statements may be enough to establish the rule; additional ones confirm it, and
may eventually exhaust it. There is no universal count at which that happens.
The editable offsets and repetition count turn the judgement into something you
can audition in this phrase instead of inheriting as advice.

Placement also changes the meaning of a transformation. A transposed cell placed
next to its source behaves as continuation. The same data after several bars can
feel like recollection. Register, cadence, and accompaniment can strengthen or
weaken that relation. Transformation functions capture local pitch and duration
rules; the `bars` plan gives those results a rhetorical position in time.

The closing bar demonstrates extension by appending C to the original cell.
Prepend the same extra note instead and the source may stop sounding like the
beginning, even though all three values remain. Recognition depends on boundary
and emphasis as well as membership, so development is partly a matter of where
the preserved material is allowed to speak.

## Take it further

Build a sixteen-bar plan from one four-note motive. Include a literal return, a
three-stage sequence, one inversion, one augmented statement, and a two-note
fragment. Derive every altered pitch list from the source rather than copying
the resulting values. Print a label before each bar, then listen without watching
the log and note which transformations announce themselves. The labels let you
compare the generated structure with the form the ear actually follows.
